title: Customer needs and building trust in a service business
audience: Owners and sales staff who plan how a service business will be found, chosen and trusted in their local market.
learningOutcomes: Describe three customer needs in observable terms
Explain why trust is the main barrier for in-home and on-site services
Test a market claim against local evidence before using it

instruction.heading: Start with what the customer is buying
instruction.body: A customer does not buy hours of work. They buy a result, a reliable arrival, and the feeling that someone they can trust is working in their home or building. The sample plan names three needs: professional conduct, convenience and trustworthiness. Turn each need into something a customer can observe. Professional conduct shows up as a punctual greeting, a tidy appearance and clear communication. Convenience shows up as booking times that suit the customer, a simple access routine and an easy way to change a visit. Trust shows up as the screening, training and damage process covered in the trust sections that follow.

instruction.heading: Trust is the main barrier
instruction.body: Many customers worry about a stranger on their property, about theft and about breakage. The sample plan reports that screening and training ease these concerns, and it treats insurance as the answer to damage a client blames on the business. Those are sensible ideas, but each claim needs evidence. Before you say that workers are screened, confirm that a screening step exists and is recorded. Before you say a loss is covered, check the policy and its limits with your insurer. A trust claim you cannot evidence damages credibility faster than making no claim at all.

instruction.heading: Trust is slow to build
instruction.body: A new business has no reviews, no referrals and no track record. The sample plan admits that goodwill takes time and that brand recognition is hard to establish at the start. Plan for that gap. Expect fewer repeat customers in the first months, budget time for follow-up with each early client, and ask every satisfied client for a referral or a review. Early clients are your evidence, so treat each job as the first step in a relationship rather than a one-off sale.

instruction.heading: Testing the market story
instruction.body: For example, a cleaning sample plan describes a market that has moved from individual housekeepers towards companies, with customers changing providers often. It also claims that some households now avoid hiring house help because of security concerns. These statements come from a plan written for another country at an unstated date, so they are hypotheses and not Australian facts. Test them locally by speaking with enough prospects and recent clients to see a pattern, choosing that number before you start. The Victorian Government's 'Who is my customer?' guidance also advises checking assumptions about buyers with research rather than guesswork, including speaking with prospects and with staff at rival businesses. Ask what they used before, what made them change, and what they would need to hear from a new provider. Record the answers with dates.

instruction.heading: Mapping competitors by type
instruction.body: The sample groups competitors into two types: individual operators who work for one or a few clients, and independent companies whose quality varies. Map your own market the same way, then add the competitors your customers name. For each type, note the price band, the trust signals it shows and the gaps you could fill. Where service quality varies widely, a consistent and documented way of working can be a real point of difference, but only if you can show it.

instruction.heading: From needs to a marketing message
instruction.body: A marketing message should answer one need, in one sentence, with proof behind it. A statement such as 'every visit follows a documented screening and damage process' has evidence behind it. A statement such as 'the best providers in town' does not. Build your message from evidence you already hold. Review the channels you use, because the sample names social platforms that may have changed since it was written. Choose channels by asking where your local customers look for a service.

procedure: List the customer's three main needs in their own words.
For each need, write the observable behaviour that shows it is being met.
Interview enough prospects or recent clients to see a pattern, and record each answer with a date.
Map the competitor types in your area and the gap each type leaves.
Turn each trust claim into a statement you can evidence, and file the evidence.
Choose one primary message and two supporting proofs for your first marketing channel.

workedExamples.situation: A two-person business in a mid-sized town wants weekly residential clients. The owner's flyer says 'we are trustworthy', but there is no written screening step, no training record and no damage process.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which trust measure should be put in place first, and what should the flyer say until it exists?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner writes a short screening and induction checklist and a damage process, then uses those on the flyer. Until they are in place, the flyer describes only what is actually done, such as a fixed arrival time and a tidy-up before leaving. The unsupported word 'trustworthy' is removed.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect interview sheet with date and source fields
Competitor map template (type, price band, trust signals, gaps)
Evidence folder for each trust claim

commonErrors.error: Making a trust claim with no record behind it
commonErrors.prevention: Attach the record, such as a checklist, certificate or policy page, before the claim is published.

commonErrors.error: Using a foreign statistic as a local fact
commonErrors.prevention: Label every external figure with its country, date and source, and test it locally before use.

commonErrors.error: Assuming customers will trust a new business quickly
commonErrors.prevention: Plan a slower early period and build a referral request into every job.
Use the same four columns for every competitor type.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Good practice: collect customer information, including names, addresses, access codes, keys and photos, only where needed, keep it secure, and do not use it for other purposes without consent. Whether the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business depends on its turnover and other factors. The OAIC's small business guidance (read in summary on 2026-11-03) says a small business with annual turnover of $3 million or less is generally exempt, although some small businesses are covered regardless of turnover. Check the OAIC page before relying on this.

Advertising claims about service results, environmental impact or safety must be true and accurate. The ACCC's guidance on false or misleading claims says claims need reasonable grounds, and a business must be able to prove a claim about a product's quality or benefit. That guidance gives no product-specific rules for cleaning products, so check each product's documentation.

qualityStandard: Each stated customer need links to a visible practice or a document.
Every trust claim on a flyer, website or quote has a matching record.
Interview notes are dated and filed, with enough responses to show a pattern before the marketing plan is finalised.
The marketing message contains no claim the business cannot evidence.
documentationEvidence: Customer needs list with the observable behaviour for each need
Dated prospect and client interview notes
Trust evidence folder covering screening, training, insurance and the damage process
summary: Customers buy a result, a reliable arrival and trust, not hours.
Trust is the main barrier, and it must be shown with records.
Trust builds slowly, so plan for the early months.
Test every market claim locally before relying on it.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which marketing trust claim is best supported?
options: Our staff are the most trustworthy in the area and our clients all say so
Our competitors are unreliable and they often miss the times they promise to clients
Every visit follows a documented screening, induction and damage process that we can show
Trust is guaranteed by our brand name and nobody can ever take that trust away from us

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does the note that trust builds slowly matter for planning?
options: It means the business should not advertise at all during the first few months of trading
It means early months may bring fewer repeat clients, so time and cash need planning
It shows that referrals work straight away from month one and the early clients always stay
It means prices should be lowest in the first year and the owner should accept any job

knowledgeChecks.question: A market statistic comes from a plan written for another country several years ago. What should the owner do?
options: Use it as a local fact for the whole plan and for every local client
Remove all market analysis from the plan and skip the rest of the research
Quote it to customers as a statistic on the website and in every advert
Treat it as a hypothesis and test it with local prospects and clients
